lines.note: Kiyō is ability or skill; the Portuguese reads Habilidade, with both medial syllables. At the far right the separate parenthesis and italic uar. are physically on this row, completing lou- in the next row; they are retained here rather than silently reordered.

Kiyo is explained by soshiri homuru, blame and praise; the Portuguese likewise gives murmuring/criticizing and praising. Its terminal lou- is completed by the displaced uar. at the right of the preceding row. The headword has no visible circumflex, unlike the preceding Qiyô.
Kiyoganna names a finishing plane. Cepilho and carpinteiros identify the tool and the carpenters; the Portuguese definition continues on the next indented physical row.

The finishing plane is used last to work and smooth the wood. The printed vltimamente, laurão and acepilhão are retained, including historical u/v usage and the two nasal marks; this is an indented continuation, not a new entry.
Kiyoganna o kakuru is to apply the finishing plane, glossed acepilhar. The paragraph sign introduces a Japanese example in roman type; only the Portuguese gloss and separator are italic.
The gloss continues with polishing the wood, completing the action of the finishing plane. There is no new headword or paragraph on this short indented row.
Kiyogaki is writing material or a model for children learning to write. The scan reads mininos, not the draft niminos; the older vowel spelling is retained rather than normalized to meninos.
The Portuguese continuation a eſcreuer completes the description of children learning to write. The tall medial letter is long s, and the historical spelling with u is retained.
Kiyoi means clean or pure, exactly the two Portuguese senses limpa and pura. This adjective begins a small group of indented derivative forms.
This indented Qiyô is the contracted adverbial form associated with kiyoi above, rather than a repetition of the ability entry at the top. The circumflex belongs to the printed Japanese form.
The noun Qiyôſa expresses cleanness/purity in this group. The tall consonant is long s, with no crossbar of f; its circumflex and derivative indentation are retained.

Kiyōjin is explained as a skillful person, qiyôna mono, then by the Portuguese person who has ability and ingenuity. The small connector is l, rather than capital I; the Japanese explanation remains roman.
Habilidade and engenho complete the Portuguese definition of the capable person. Both nouns are printed italic; no Japanese word is embedded on this continuation.
Kiyome, uru, eta gives the verb to clean, glossed Alimpar. The paragraph then starts the Japanese example Quai-, continued by qe on the next row; the physical word division must remain.
Quai-qe uo qiyomuru is glossed taking revenge, followed by Fagiuo, beginning another expression for clearing shame. The gap between qe and uo is visible; Vingarſe has long s, not f.
Fagi uo qiyomuru receives the same revenge gloss, Idem. A further paragraph starts Miuo qiyomu-, purifying oneself, with its final ru on the next row.
The roman ru completes qiyomuru. Portuguese gives washing or purifying oneself, then begins another purification sense with Puri-; the two typefaces distinguish the Japanese ending from the gloss.

Purification is specified as doing penance and observing continence. The printed abbreviation continẽ ends this physical row without a supplied hyphen; its nasal bar is retained before cia on the following row.
The first cia completes continẽcia. Cocorouo qiyomuru then means purifying the heart; the Portuguese A- is the start of Apurar on the next row and remains here.
Purar completes Apurar, followed by cleansing the heart. The cedilla and nasal sign in coração are visible and are retained in this wholly Portuguese continuation.
Kiyōna and kiyōjin describe a skillful, ingenious person. The scan has habil, not babil; the beta-shaped double-s sort in Peßoa and the divided en-genho are retained.
Genho completes engenho, the ingenuity of the person described immediately above. This short row is a Portuguese continuation, not a separate Japanese form.
Qiyôni is the indented adverbial form, skillfully, belonging to the ability group rather than the earlier purity group. Its roman typography and circumflex are explicit.
Qiyôſa is the corresponding noun for skill or ability here. Its identical spelling to the earlier purity noun is retained; position within the entry group distinguishes the senses.

runs.text: O deſagradar algũa couſa a alguem.

lines.note: Kizakai is displeasure or something displeasing a person. The headword has z, not the draft t; the scan and its adjoining adjective/adverb group agree. Portuguese retains algũa and long s in deſagradar and couſa.
Kizakaina describes something disagreeable. The initial is Q rather than D, matching the base noun above and the adverb below; the gloss likewise says a thing that displeases.
Qizacaini is the adverb of the same displeasure group, explicitly labelled Adu. The headword is roman and the grammatical label italic; no extra gloss is supplied.
Kizahashi is a stair or steps, matched by Degraos da eſcada. The older headword has f for the historical h sound and x for sh; neither is modernized.

runs.text: Riquezas como peças de prata, alfa-

lines.note: Kizai denotes wealth or valuables. Portuguese specifies silver pieces and begins alfa-yas, valuable possessions, divided across the physical rows.
Yas completes alfayas, concluding the list of valuables. The short indented continuation and final &c. are retained rather than joined to the preceding line.
Kizami is a time or occasion here, glossed Hora, ou conjunção. The example begins Vonme-, the first part of onme ni kakatta, meeting or appearing before someone.

The initial is read ni, the particle after Vonme- on the preceding row, rather than draft ui. Its n is abraded to two stems, so this individual glyph remains a nonblocking graphic uncertainty; the Japanese onme ni kakatta kizami ni and Portuguese Naquelle comenos support the chosen reading.

runs.text: ou hora, em que me apreſentei a voßos olhos.

lines.note: The Portuguese completes the time-of-meeting example: the hour when I presented myself before your eyes. The last noun is olhos, not olbos; the damaged italic h still has its descending shoulder, and voßos retains its beta-shaped double-s.
Qizami, u, ǒda gives the verb to cut or chop, glossed cutting something finely. The caron over ǒ is visible; the historical principal parts and abbreviated algũa are retained.

runs.text: couſa. ¶ Item, Abrir algũa couſa em pe-

lines.note: The first couſa completes the cutting gloss. A new paragraph introduces engraving or incising in pe-dra, so the final pe- belongs to the Portuguese stone word continued below.
Stone and metal complete the engraving materials. Ixini monjiuo qi- begins the Japanese example of carving characters in stone; the roman ending qi- is not part of the italic Portuguese.

runs.text: Abrir, ou talhar letras em pedra.

lines.note: Zamu completes kizamu in the Japanese example. Abrir, ou talhar letras em pedra gives carving letters in stone, confirming the verb and the physical word division.

Shatō ni in o kizamu kamome describes gulls imprinting marks on a sandy shore; the following Portuguese explains their tracks. Feiq. is a separate roman citation label, not part of the example; the caron in Xatǒ is visible.

runs.text: As gaiuotas que deixauão as pegadas na area.

lines.note: The Portuguese explains the literary image as gulls leaving footprints in sand. Deixauão is retained as printed, without normalizing the older ending or the spelling area.
Kizamitçuke is to engrave or carve something onto a surface. The printed tç cluster and the principal parts uru, eta are retained; eſcul- continues onto the next line.
Pir completes eſculpir. The example Monjiuo qizami tçu- concerns engraving characters, with the separated verb elements and end-of-line hyphen preserved.
Quru completes tçuquru in the preceding example; the Portuguese specifies carving letters in stone or wood. The scan has pao without an added nasal mark.

runs.text: Certa laya de figos de Iapão.

lines.note: Kizawashi is identified as a kind of Japanese fig. The scan reads Qi-, not Qu-; the supplied lexical index agrees with Qizauaxi. The gloss uses historical laya and Iapão.
Qizaxi, ſu, aita means sprouting or budding. Portuguese begins with herbs and go-mos, buds, while the Japanese x and the long s of ſu are distinct printed letters.

runs.text: mos, ou folhas nouas de aruore, &c. ¶

lines.note: Mos completes gomos; leaves of a tree extend the botanical gloss. A new paragraph begins Mǒ-, the start of mōnen, with the caron and printed division preserved.
Mǒ-nenga qizaſu applies sprouting figuratively to thoughts. Per met. and Aleuantaremſe introduce the figurative Portuguese explanation; the Japanese is roman and the gloss italic.
Ruins penſamentos completes the explanation as bad thoughts arising. The long s in penſamentos is retained, and this is the final body row of the first column.

Kizashi here concerns disposition, illustrated by kizashi no yoi hito, a person of good disposition. The initial Q and the rest of the headword are one roman word, not an italic O plus izaxi; the example also has z rather than draft c.
De boa condição completes the description of the good-natured person. The final nasal spelling and the wholly italic Portuguese continuation are retained.

runs.text: Familia, ou gẽte nobre como de Cun-

lines.note: Kizoku denotes noble family or people. Portuguese introduces Cungues as an example of aristocratic status, dividing the embedded Japanese-derived title as Cun-gues across rows; the vowel in Cun- is read as u from its open top.
Gues completes the title Cungues within the Portuguese definition of noble families. This is an embedded Japanese term, unlike a standalone Japanese synonym or example.
Kizu is a cut or wound. Kizuuo begins the expression to receive a wound; the apparent final l in the draft is the right column rule, not a letter, and has been removed.
Cǒmuru completes kizu o kōmuru, receiving a wound, as the Portuguese confirms. The paragraph then opens another sense with the printed abbreviated Itẽ.
The figurative sense is infamy or a defect. Nani tçuita qi- begins a Japanese example about a blemish attached to a name, continuing across the next physical row.

runs.text: zuua matdai madeua yomo vxeji. Yax.

lines.note: The example says a stain on a name will not disappear even in later ages. The historical matdai and word spacing are retained; Yax. is the separate roman source label, not the end of the Japanese sentence.

runs.text: A infamia, ou nodoa que ſe poem no nome

lines.note: The Portuguese translates the Japanese stigma image as infamy or a stain put on a name. Poem and nodoa retain their printed unaccented forms rather than receiving modern diacritics.

runs.text: não ſe apaga jà mais pera ſempre. ¶

lines.note: The gloss says the stain is never erased. The printed jà mais remains two words with its visible accent; after the paragraph sign, Qizu- starts a new wound-healing example.
Kizuuo iyaſu means healing a wound, glossed Curar a ferida. The second Qizuuo begins a separate example, so the two Japanese spans must not be conflated with the intervening italic gloss.

runs.text: Dar ferida, ou fazer ſinal, ou

lines.note: Tçuquru completes the example making or inflicting a wound. Portuguese extends the sense to making a mark, with the final ou introducing the next row.
The continuation adds a notch or dent made with iron. The printed mòça has both a grave accent and a cedilla; the physical line contains only Portuguese.
Kizui is explained by kidoku as a miracle or marvel. Qidocu after i, is an ordinary Japanese synonym in roman type, not a Japanese word embedded inside the Portuguese explanation.
Kizui no genzuru is glossed performing miracles. The printed no is retained even though modern phrasing might differ; this is a standalone Japanese example followed by an italic gloss.

runs.text: O ſer de ſua vontade liure, & abſoluto.

lines.note: This second Kizui means acting freely according to one’s own will, rather than a miracle. The Portuguese liure and abſoluto preserve historical spelling and long s.

runs.text: Peßoa amiga de ſeu proprio parecer,

lines.note: Kizuina describes someone attached to their own opinion. The beta-shaped double-s in Peßoa is visible; proprio remains unaccented as in the print.
The Portuguese continues the characterization as fashioned to one’s own will. The grave on à is visible and retained, and the line remains an indented continuation.
Qizuini is the corresponding adverb, explicitly labelled Adu. The line has no additional example or translated definition to supply.

Kizuyamai concerns a troublesome wound condition; the example describes a person who has it. The supposed gap after initial Q in the draft is ordinary letter spacing, so Qizuyamaiuo is one roman word.

runs.text: Homem que ſàra difficultoſamente da ferida

lines.note: The example is glossed as a man who heals with difficulty from a wound. The accent in ſàra and the long-s sorts are retained rather than normalized to modern Portuguese.

runs.text: por cauſa do ferro lhe ſer contrario, ou ter ru-

lines.note: The historical explanation attributes difficult healing to iron being contrary to the person or to ru-im carnadura. This is the source’s medical description, retained without endorsing or updating it.
Im carnadura completes ruim carnadura, referring to poorly healing flesh in the preceding gloss. The short italic continuation is preserved as a physical row.

Kizukushini is labelled an adverb and explained by Cocorouo tçuca-, continued by the printed racaite on the next row. The Japanese explanation concerns exhausting the heart or mind, consistent with the Portuguese distress and anguish; its apparent missing consonant is documented below rather than silently supplied.

The separate second pass and enlarged native scan show racaite, with no x between a and i. This printed anomaly is retained: racaxite would be a contextual emendation, not a transcription of the visible letters. Portuguese reads affliçaõ, with two f letters and the nasal mark over final o, followed by anguish; the draft’s afiniçaãõ is unsupported.
Kizzucuxini iranu cotouo ſuna warns against unnecessary activities undertaken in distress. The italic Não begins the Portuguese translation after the complete roman imperative.

runs.text: façais couſas eſcuſadas com afflição matando-

lines.note: The Portuguese continues: do not do unnecessary things with distress, wearing yourselves out. The printed afflição here has its nasal mark on a, unlike affliçaõ two rows earlier; matando- continues below.
Uos completes matando-uos, the reflexive expression about exhausting oneself. The initial u is retained as printed rather than replaced by modern v; the row concludes the previous example.
Kizukai denotes distress, pain, or worries. The initial Q is part of the headword, not a separated character; the second occurrence begins Qiz- and continues zucaiuo on the next row.
Qiz-zucaiuo ſuru means having worries or taking something to heart. The Portuguese confirms the sense with Ter cuidados, ou tomar pena; the Japanese remains roman.

Fitoni qizzucaiuo caquru means causing someone worry or distress. Dar pena begins the matching Portuguese explanation; the damaged letters in pena are resolved by their surviving strokes and the following cuidados.
The Portuguese adds causing cares to someone, completing the preceding example. The spelling alguem is unaccented in this row, and no new paragraph is present.
Kizumari is an oppressive or constricted feeling in the heart. Abafamento de coração is the Portuguese definition; the damaged middle of abafamento does not change the word.

runs.text: O eſtar com o coração a bafa-

lines.note: Kizumarina describes being oppressed at heart. The initial is Q, not draft G; the source’s space in a bafa- is retained rather than silently joining abafado across its printed word and line divisions.
Do completes a bafa-do. The Japanese Qizzumarina coto then introduces a thing or circumstance that causes this oppressive feeling; Couſa de opens its Portuguese gloss.
The gloss describes oppression and constriction of the heart. Both nouns and the conjunction belong to the italic Portuguese continuation, not to a new Japanese entry.

Qizzumarini is the adverb belonging to the preceding adjective. The final i is faint but visible before the period; the supplied lexical index agrees, whereas the draft omitted it. Aduer. is the printed grammatical label.

runs.text: O trazer ſempre, ou de còte veſti

lines.note: Kizume denotes wearing clothes or arms continually. The whole headword is roman Qizzume, not an italic O followed by izzume; the Portuguese has còte with a grave and ends veſti without a visible hyphen.
Dos completes veſtidos, followed by arms as another thing worn. Cono qirumonouo begins the Japanese example about wearing this garment; the source spelling qirumono is retained.
Qizzumeni xiteua varucarǒ says it would be bad to keep this garment in continual wear. The final caron in varucarǒ and the Portuguese Naõ with its mark over o are both retained.

runs.text: trazer ſempre eſte veſtido de cǒte.

lines.note: The Portuguese completes the statement that it is not good to wear this garment continually. Enlargement shows an unmistakable two-stroke caron over o in cǒte; this unusual Portuguese diacritic is retained, not normalized to the còte printed above.

The new section begins Qua, fire, explained by Japanese fi and Portuguese Fogo. The large Q belongs to this row and spans two lines; it was omitted by the OCR. Fǔ, qua gives wind and fire, matching the split Portuguese gloss Vẽto / & fogo.
The Portuguese & fogo completes wind and fire. This row is indented beside the descending tail of the enlarged Q above; that initial is not a second character belonging to this row.

Qua is a fault or sin, explained by toga and Peccado. The print tightly joins Maisſe, with short s followed by long s, not draft Mairſe; it says the form Zai-qua is more usual. The hyphen belongs to the roman Japanese word.

Qua completes Zaiqua. The example concerns failing to correct an error; the ending is read cotouo, not corouo, from the surviving t and Japanese koto o. The sentence runs onward beyond this page; no continuation is invented.

The isolated bottom-right quato is treated as catchword furniture from its position below the final body row. A short, nearly upright stroke immediately before it is read as an opening parenthesis; its exact shape is uncertain. The following f405 was not supplied, and an attempted Gallica retrieval failed, so repetition there and this role could not be independently confirmed. Both the visible word and its preceding mark are retained rather than discarded or joined to the body sentence.
